paragraphs: This list is for self-questioning only and does not constitute recruitment criteria, a capability score, or an evaluation of investigation and forensic conclusions. This page is written according to the US O*NET-SOC 19-4092.00 'Forensic Science Technicians' (the fixed index gives this asset the Chinese name whose English rendering is 'Forensic science technicians'; the main objects are collecting, identifying, classifying and analysing physical evidence related to criminal cases, examining materials such as weapons or fibres and hair and tissue, possibly testifying in court as an expert witness on evidence or crime laboratory techniques, and possibly specialising in fields such as ballistics, fingerprints, handwriting or biochemistry).

Paper exercise | use the complete fictional input of F-01 in the entry exercise on this page, and within 90 minutes check the E01/E02 seals and handover, calculate the E01 mean and relative difference, and identify that batch B blanks exceed the limit and correct the old report. Deliver the evidence list, quality control sheet, anomaly record and a bounded summary; the reference answer, time allocation and marking are given in the same section. Do not handle real samples or hazardous materials.

Fit signals | O*NET points of focus: face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (86%), using email every day (82%), an extremely important impact of decisions on colleagues and unit results (73%), precision or accuracy extremely important (67%), some freedom to determine tasks and priorities (66%), in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment every day (60%), some decision freedom (55%), more than 40 hours of work (48%), handling, controlling or feeling objects and tools with the hands more than half the time every day (48%). If you are willing to collect and examine physical evidence carefully to procedure and can switch between scene and laboratory while keeping records accurate, the daily requirements of this occupation are closer to your way of working.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows: the consequences of error are extremely serious (47%), exposed to contaminants every day (36%), wearing routine protective or safety equipment every day (36%), outdoors exposed to all weather every day (43%), working in enclosed or awkward positions once a week or more (45%), exposed to distracting noise once a week or more (37%), dealing with unpleasant or angry or discourteous people once a week or more (31%), public speaking every day (31%), exposed to disease or infection once a month or more (47%). Examination errors or a break in the chain of evidence can directly affect cases and the people involved, and the scene and laboratory involve biological and chemical and sharps and equipment risks. If you find it hard to bear strict procedures and consequential responsibility, or are uncomfortable about biological and chemical and hazardous material exposure, treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Taking on the judgement | verify three types of task against the target position: scene collection, sealing and handover; laboratory methods, quality control and result records; report review, result interpretation and possible court appearances. Institutions may divide the work, and no single technician can be required to carry all the steps in the same case. First complete the fictional record and quality control exercise on this page and observe accuracy, anomaly identification and explanation habits; real scenes, laboratory operations and assessment take place only under lawful teaching or institutional authorisation, and neither the exercise nor an interest questionnaire constitutes a recruitment or competence conclusion.

Paper exercise | use the complete fictional input of F-01 in the entry exercise on this page, and within 90 minutes check the E01/E02 seals and handover, calculate the E01 mean and relative difference, and identify that batch B blanks exceed the limit and correct the old report. Deliver the evidence list, quality control sheet, anomaly record and a bounded summary; the reference answer, time allocation and marking are given in the same section. Do not handle real samples or hazardous materials.

Occupational scope | according to the US O*NET-SOC19-4092.00, collect, identify, classify and analyse physical evidence related to criminal investigations; examine weapons, fibres, hair, tissue and so on, explain their significance to the investigation, and possibly specialise in areas such as ballistics, fingerprints, handwriting or biochemistry and testify in court. Scene and laboratory positions may be divided, and no individual can be required to cover all exhibits. The occupational classification itself does not confer investigation, medical diagnosis or legal adjudication authority, nor does it wholly prohibit examining personnel with the corresponding qualifications from signing opinions; the specific scope of examination, review, sign-off and testimony depends on local systems and institutional authorisation.

entries: Scene examination and evidence collection | source and location and time | collect, package and preserve physical evidence to procedure, recording the source and location and time and maintaining the chain of evidence.

Laboratory examination and analysis | methods and result records | examine physical evidence such as fibres and hair and biological samples or firearms and ballistics or fingerprints and footprints using standard methods and record it truthfully.
Records and reports | reports and charts and photographs | write records and reports and organise charts and photographs and examination method details to support review and traceability.

Court testimony and expert opinion | explaining methods and conclusions | give evidence in court as an expert witness on examination methods and results and discuss evidence interpretation with experts in other fields where necessary.
Equipment and reagents and safety | operation and maintenance | operate and maintain laboratory equipment, prepare and use reagents and handle hazardous materials and biological samples to procedure.
Databases and collaboration and training | entry and mentoring | enter and query databases, collaborate with investigation and forensic and judicial personnel and train new staff and others.

paragraphs:
Work context | the O*NET 19-4092.00 work context shows (the percentages are respondent distributions, not individual working hours or accident rates): the work combines scene examination and laboratory examination, with high procedural and accuracy requirements.
Communication and collaboration | face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams every day (86%), using email every day (82%), working with a team extremely important (47%), leading or coordinating others extremely important (42%).

External contact and testimony | public speaking every day (31%), dealing with unpleasant or angry or discourteous people at least once a week but not every day (31%), conflict situations once a year or more but not monthly (32%).
Environmental conditions | in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment every day (60%), outdoors exposed to all weather every day (43%), working outdoors in a sheltered place at least once a week but not every day (46%).

Lighting and temperature | exposed to extremely bright or inadequate lighting every day (32%), exposed to very hot or very cold temperatures every day (29%), indoors not environmentally controlled never (26%).

Hazard exposure | exposed to contaminants every day (36%), wearing routine protective or safety equipment every day (36%), working in enclosed or awkward positions at least once a week but not every day (45%), exposed to distracting noise at least once a week but not every day (37%), exposed to disease or infection at least once a month but not every week (47%).

Precision and decisions | precision or accuracy extremely important (67%), a very important impact of decisions on colleagues and unit results (73%), the consequences of error extremely serious (47%), some freedom to determine tasks and priorities (66%), some decision freedom (55%).
Time and physical | time pressure at least once a week but not every day (37%), more than 40 hours of work (48%), handling, controlling or feeling objects and tools more than half the time (48%), sitting about half the time (61%), standing less than half the time (29%).
Responsibility and collaboration results | limited responsibility for the work results of others (31%), moderate responsibility for the health and safety of others (33%).

Environment and pace | the scene and laboratory may be divided. O*NET60% of respondents answered an enclosed vehicle or equipment every day, 43% outdoor weather every day, 46% outdoor shelter at least once a week but not every day, 36% contaminants every day, 47% disease exposure at least once a month but not every week; 37% time pressure at least once a week but not every day, 48% a typical working week over 40 hours, 48% handling objects more than half the time. These are respondent distributions, not individual working hours or accident rates, and are not enough to summarise the work as moderately physical or as long periods of standing. The OOH notes that most laboratories work normal hours, with some extended, non-standard or district scene attendance; actual conditions are verified by position.

Tools and materials | use scene photography, measurement, fingerprint processing, laboratory instruments, databases, packaging and seals and safety protection according to your specialism. O*NET also lists drone image collection as an added task, which is not required in all positions. The specific reagents, storage conditions and equipment parameters must follow the institution's valid SOP, and this page is not an operating procedure.

Scene examination and collection → packaging and preservation and handover → laboratory examination and equipment and reagents → records and reports and charts → review and method explanation → court testimony and archiving

Quality and records | editorial review suggestion: the source, location, collection time, sealing and handover should be traceable; methods, quality control, equipment status, anomalies and uncertainty must be recorded truthfully. Anomalies are escalated per the institution's SOP and must not be falsified after the fact; lawful corrections should retain the original value, the reason, the time and the responsible person. Sign-off is carried by those with the corresponding qualifications and authorisation.

Adjacent positions | medical laboratory work mainly supports diagnosis and treatment; criminal investigation focuses on investigative leads; fire investigation focuses on fire cause and fire safety inspection. Police identification personnel also handle physical evidence and fingerprints and testify; private investigation may also involve criminal cases. The work overlaps, so the specific tasks, exhibits and appointment must be verified, and the occupational classification on this page is not treated as exclusive authority.

Boundary review points | pause and escalate when the following arise: a break or damage in the chain of evidence or seals; storage conditions or time beyond the limit that may affect results; examination results that are abnormal or seriously inconsistent with expectations; contamination or sample mixing or equipment anomalies that may interfere with conclusions; biological and chemical and sharps exposure or personnel injury; and any situation that may affect the forensic opinion or requires re-examination. These are handled by qualified personnel, the laboratory manager and the corresponding institution per procedure and regulations.
Scene collection → packaging and preservation → laboratory examination → records and reports → review and explanation → court and archiving

Difference from detectives-and-criminal-investigators: the latter are responsible for case investigation and interviewing and the use of evidence and investigative direction judgements; this occupation is responsible for the collection, examination and recording of physical evidence and the explanation of results, providing technical conclusions for investigation and judicial use, and the occupational classification itself does not confer investigative decision authority; those appointed as police officers or holding other authority are verified by actual duties, and are not excluded wholesale by title.

Difference from medical-and-clinical-laboratory-technicians: the latter examine clinical samples to support disease diagnosis and treatment; this occupation examines case physical evidence to support investigation and justice, and the sample types, procedures, use of results and court requirements differ.

Comparison points | adjacent positions are compared by main object and authority; police identification personnel also examine physical evidence and testify, and private investigators may also be involved in criminal cases. Medical laboratories use clinical samples to support diagnosis and criminal investigation centres on case leads; titles and tasks overlap, and position authority must be verified separately.

Adjacent boundaries | police identification and records personnel (O*NET33-3021.02) also handle physical evidence at the scene or in the laboratory, classify and identify fingerprints, take photographs, write records and testify, overlapping with this occupation in both tasks and position titles; the difference must be verified in terms of occupational classification, specific specialism, whether they are police officers and institutional appointment, and it cannot be said that they only keep files or that their examination is limited in depth. Private investigators, by contrast, collect, analyse and report personal or organisational information for clients, and may obtain evidence and testify in criminal or civil cases, not only in civil commercial matters.

Before choosing this occupation, compare: the real tasks (the share of scene examination and laboratory examination and reports and testimony and equipment maintenance), qualification and training paths (relevant degree and on-the-job training and proficiency assessment and state or institutional credentials), working conditions and responsibility (non-standard hours and scene attendance, hazardous materials and biological exposure, extremely serious consequences of error), and growth paths (scene technician, laboratory specialism direction, independent case handling after proficiency assessment, senior technical and quality or training positions). Employers vary considerably (federal, state and local law enforcement agencies, forensic institutions and private laboratories) and this should be verified against actual recruitment and on-site experience.

Responsibility boundaries cannot be inferred from the similarity of job titles: although all are law enforcement and examination positions, investigation and interviewing, patrol and scene handling, identification and records, fire investigation, private investigation, clinical examination and physical evidence examination differ in authority and outputs. Cross-position work requires relearning procedures and qualifications and evidence requirements, and the original position's judgement and sign-off authority cannot be carried over; matters involving the issue of forensic opinions and case conclusions and legal application must be borne by qualified personnel and the corresponding institution.

AI task exposure | digital tools may assist with organising and annotating scene photographs and video, database search and comparison, preliminary instrument data processing and image enhancement, report templates and chart generation, and case archiving and statistics. But scene collection and packaging and preservation, examination methods and result determination, chain of evidence maintenance, and result interpretation and court testimony remain the responsibility of technicians and qualified personnel; task exposure does not equal job replacement, and tool outputs cannot replace a reviewable explanation of the method.

Occupational definition | according to the US O*NET-SOC19-4092.00, collect, identify, classify and analyse physical evidence related to criminal investigations; examine weapons, fibres, hair, tissue and so on, explain their significance to the investigation, and possibly specialise in areas such as ballistics, fingerprints, handwriting or biochemistry and testify in court. Scene and laboratory positions may be divided, and no individual can be required to cover all exhibits. The occupational classification itself does not confer investigation, medical diagnosis or legal adjudication authority, nor does it wholly prohibit examining personnel with the corresponding qualifications from signing opinions; the specific scope of examination, review, sign-off and testimony depends on local systems and institutional authorisation.

Data and system thresholds | before adoption, verify: whether examination data can be traced back to the instrument and batch and method version and personnel; whether tools are validated versions with change records; the permissions and retention periods and encryption requirements for case and party information; the data consistency and audit trails of interfaces with the laboratory information management system and law enforcement databases; and whether procedures allow degraded operation while retaining original records during system failure.

Human control points and manual review | scene collection and packaging and preservation, examination method selection and result determination, the chain of evidence and storage conditions, report and conclusion wording, court testimony, and hazardous material and biosafety handling must be completed by technicians and qualified personnel; any comparison result, image enhancement, preliminary identification or report draft generated by a tool must be manually checked with a trace left before use.

Residual responsibility | matters that must not be released automatically: whether the physical evidence is in its original state with an intact chain, whether the examination method is applicable and validated, whether the results involve interference or uncertainty, whether the conclusion wording matches the evidence, and decisions involving re-examination and changes to the forensic opinion. No tool output equals a forensic conclusion or an authorisation decision.

Failure risk | unreviewed tool outputs may cause false comparisons and misidentification, image enhancement artefacts misread as findings, distorted results and uncertainty wording, missing chain of evidence records, and leakage of case information, creating forensic error and judicial consequences and compliance risk. Before deployment, make clear who reviews and against what original data and procedures.

Employment evidence boundaries | the employment and wage data of this occupation must be distinguished by definition: the US figures from O*NET and the BLS are estimates under a specific statistical definition and cannot be extrapolated directly to mainland China or other regions; China uses industry category average wages as a background proxy, which does not constitute an occupational wage conclusion. Anything generated should be traceable back to the original inputs and sources, and fluent wording must not be treated as correct evidence.

Exploration suggestion | photographs, data processing and report assistance are not automatically low risk; first observe errors on fictional materials, and handle real materials only under institutional authorisation, validation and traceability requirements, retaining originals, parameters and correction records. Tool effectiveness and adoption were not verified, and being rollback-capable does not mean the integrity of evidence is unaffected.

US OEWS estimates by SOC occupation, and the two have different coverage, so they are not spliced or converted and industry averages are not substituted for occupational wages.

paragraphs: Comparison conclusion | occupational classifications are divided by main task: clinical examination serves medicine, criminal investigation focuses on leads and investigation, and fire investigation focuses on cause and fire safety inspection; police identification personnel overlap with this occupation in physical evidence, fingerprints and testimony. Private investigation may also serve criminal cases. Specific authority depends on the appointment, and substitutability cannot be judged from the title.

Evidence note | the comparison objects in the table below come from the O*NET occupational classification and current public occupational materials, and are used to help distinguish the work content of adjacent occupations and choose a fit; they do not constitute qualification, recruitment or compensation conclusions. The wages and employment of each occupation must be verified separately under their own SOC definitions, and this table does not compare figures or treat one occupation's wage as a proxy for another's.

Preface | the following comparison is laid out in four columns: 'occupational direction — core work and outputs — key differences — what it is a better choice for'. Law enforcement and examination scenes are often linked by process, but linkage does not equal substitutability; when choosing across directions, the procedures, qualifications and evidence requirements must be relearned.

Centred on the collection, examination and reporting of case physical evidence: collect, package and preserve at the scene to procedure, examine fibres and hair and biological samples or firearms and ballistics or fingerprints and footprints in the laboratory using standard methods, write reports and charts, and give evidence in court as an expert witness on methods and conclusions when necessary.

Better suited to people willing to collect and examine physical evidence carefully to procedure, who can switch between scene and laboratory, and who can bear accuracy and consequential responsibility.

Output is technical conclusions usable for investigation and justice: scene examination and handover records, examination method and result records, reports and charts and photographs, and the method explanation given in court testimony.
This occupation: forensic science technicians

Centred on clinical sample examination to support diagnosis and treatment: examination of blood and body fluid and tissue samples, instrument and reagent operation and quality control, and release of results and clinical communication.
Better suited to people whose focus is clinical examination and quality control; those who prefer case physical evidence and court explanations fit this occupation.

Output is clinical examination results and reports: sample examination and quality control records, result reports and critical value communication, and instrument maintenance and calibration records.
Medical and Clinical Laboratory Technicians

Centred on case investigation and interviewing and the use of evidence: case analysis and lead tracking, interviewing and evidence gathering and coercive measures, and investigative direction and building the chain of evidence.
Better suited to people who take on investigative decisions and interviewing and evidence gathering; those who prefer laboratory examination and technical conclusions fit this occupation.
Output is investigative results: leads and the chain of evidence, interview and evidence gathering records, and case investigation reports.
Detectives and Criminal Investigators
Centred on fire cause and hazard investigation: fire scene examination and cause determination, fire safety installation and hazard inspection, and inspection and rectification and incident records.
Better suited to people whose professional direction is fire investigation and fire safety inspection; those who prefer physical evidence laboratory examination and testimony fit this occupation.
Output is fire investigation and inspection conclusions: fire cause and scene records, hazard inspection and rectification records, and incident and investigation conclusions.
Fire Inspectors and Investigators

Collect, classify and process physical evidence at the scene and in the laboratory, identify fingerprints, take photographs and maintain records, and may testify; the tasks overlap with this occupation and must be compared by position appointment and specialism.
Those interested in scene identification, fingerprint or records work can compare this direction; it cannot be inferred from the job title alone that they have no examination responsibility.
Outputs include scene physical evidence, fingerprint processing, imagery, records and testimony; it is not only identity verification files.
Police Identification and Records Officers

Collect, analyse and report personal or organisational information for clients and investigate unlawful or irregular events in private organisations; they may also gather evidence and testify in civil and criminal cases.
Better suited to people focused mainly on civil and commercial investigation and information verification; those who prefer laboratory examination and court testimony fit this occupation.
Output is investigation results: investigation and interview records, material and evidence verification, and investigation reports and client feedback.
Private Detectives and Investigators

Transition | this page sets adjacent positions side by side by 'authority and outputs', to help you judge which kind of law enforcement and examination scene you want to invest in long term. Whichever direction you choose, what really determines whether you can take up the work is your understanding of procedures and evidence and safety requirements, your ability to stay accurate and reviewable in high-consequence situations, and passing the institution's and laboratory's qualification and proficiency assessment; an interest questionnaire is only for raising questions.

What should you prepare before entering? values: Purely paper-based fictional prompt: teaching task F-01, not corresponding to a real case, with no real individuals, exhibits, firearms, reagents or equipment. E01 is a paper record of blue fibres at point P1, registered by person A at 09:10, seal S01; at 09:30 A handed over to B with complete records on both sides, and at 10:00 B handed over to C with complete records. E02 is a paper record of red fibres at point P2, registered by A at 09:20, seal S02; at 10:05 C found the seal damaged, and the 09:40 handover column lacks the recipient. All times are on the same fictional date.

Simulated method M-1 is an arithmetic exercise only: blank readings should be ≤0.020; the standard reading is 0.100 with a permissible range of 0.090—0.110; and for samples the relative difference of the two readings = absolute value of the difference ÷ mean × 100%, which should be ≤10%. The values are dimensionless; they do not correspond to real forensic thresholds and no reagent preparation is required.

Batch A: blank 0.010, standard 0.100, E01 readings 0.080 and 0.084; batch B: blank 0.030, standard 0.100, E02 readings 0.120 and 0.118. Anomalies have been deliberately planted. The two readings and their mean cannot prove that fibres come from the same source, or establish identity or case facts.

The old draft awaiting review says 'E01 and E02 are both valid, E02 matches source X, and the handover is complete'. No comparison sample is provided for source X. Review using only the inputs of this task and do not invent missing records. The tool is pen and paper or a spreadsheet calculator, with a 90 minute limit.

Deliverables: the E01/E02 evidence list and handover check sheet, the quality control judgement for the two batches, the E01 mean and relative difference calculation, the E02 anomaly register, the item-by-item correction of the old report and a bounded result summary.

For each record write the number, point, known time, responsible role, seal status and whether the record is missing; write unknown where there is no value. Write out the steps to pause, report to the fictional supervisor and preserve the original records, without adding signatures or backfilling.

90 minute allocation: 15 minutes input checks, 20 minutes list and handover, 20 minutes arithmetic quality control, 20 minutes report correction, 10 minutes anomaly escalation, 5 minutes self-check. This practises records only, not real examination or forensic sign-off.

Reference answer | the E01 list and handover are complete as regards the given records; batch A blank 0.010 ≤ 0.020 and standard 0.100 within the permissible range. Mean (0.080+0.084)/2 = 0.082; relative difference 0.004 / 0.082 × 100% = 4.878% (about 4.88%), passing this task's 10% condition. Passing simulated quality control does not equal a valid real forensic examination.

Reference answer | the E02 seal is damaged and the 09:40 recipient is unknown, so record the anomaly and pause reporting a definite result in this exercise, retain the original entries and report to the fictional supervisor for checking; batch B blank 0.030 > 0.020, which fails. A passing standard does not offset a failed blank; even if the two readings are close, it cannot be released.

Old report correction | 'both valid', 'handover complete' and 'matches source X' do not hold. Change to: E01 completed the simulated arithmetic check, and E02 awaits review because of the chain and blank anomalies; no comparison sample for X was provided, so a match, common source or guilt cannot be determined. The correction retains the old values, the reason, the time and the review role.

Self-check marking (editorial rules, 20 points) | input list and handover 6 points, mean and relative difference 4 points, identifying the blank and seal anomalies 4 points, three corrections to the old report 4 points, and making the fiction and authority clear 2 points. If you miss the E02 suspension, add fabricated signatures or infer a source from the readings, rework it first; the score is not an occupational qualification or recruitment threshold.

All data and thresholds are fictional and can only verify records and arithmetic; they must not be applied to any real sample, case or laboratory instrument. Real examination, re-examination, evidence handling and sign-off for anomalies follow institutional SOP and the law, and no authorisation is obtained from this task.

Use only the paper materials in this task; do not collect human materials, handle hazardous reagents or weapons, or import real cases or external services. The work can only show that one learning exercise was completed and cannot be written up as casework, certification or laboratory experience.

entries.answer: The O*NET work context shows: face-to-face discussion with individuals and teams every day 86%, using email every day 82%, an extremely important impact of decisions on colleagues and unit results 73%, precision or accuracy extremely important 67%, in an enclosed vehicle or enclosed equipment every day 60%, outdoor exposure every day 43%, exposed to contaminants every day 36%, wearing protective equipment every day 36%, exposed to disease or infection more than once a month 47%, the consequences of error extremely serious 47%, and more than 40 hours of work 48%. Scene and laboratory work coexist, and procedures and protective equipment and occupational health management can reduce the risk, but biological and chemical exposure and consequential pressure are real costs.

entries.answer: This page proposes possible tool support directions from the tasks and obtained no AI exposure level, adoption rate or replacement year for this occupation; ordinary instrument software and generative AI must not be conflated. Actual use requires verification of method validation, original data, privacy, review and sign-off responsibility; no promise is made that replacement will not occur in the short term, and employment causation is not inferred from a technology demonstration.

entries.answer: The O*NET answers on the education needed by newly hired workers are postsecondary certificate 36% and high school or equivalent 29%; these are shares of answers about the education needed, not the education distribution of existing or newly hired workers (the page lists only these two percentages); the Job Zone is 3 (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); the BLS states that a bachelor's degree is usually required (physical science, biology or forensic science direction), that some positions accept a college diploma, and that on-the-job training and proficiency assessment are required. Actual requirements are subject to the employer and position requirements and local rules.
entries.question: What education and training are required?

entries.answer: The US OOH states that certification is usually not a uniform entry requirement, and independent cases may require a proficiency examination or institutional approval; some police officer positions separately require police training. China check | under the judicial administration registration system, a forensic examiner must be registered and work within the practice category and the institution's scope; the General Rules on Forensic Examination Procedure provide for review, examiner signature and institutional seal. Public security organs have a separate 2020 examiner registration measure, and the two routes must not be conflated. A degree, an assistant position or institutional training does not automatically become examiner status; those with qualifications and authorisation can bear sign-off responsibility.
entries.question: Are certificates or qualifications required?

entries.answer: Common failures include: incomplete collection and sealing and handover records leading to doubt about the chain of evidence, improper methods or misjudged results and unidentified interference leading to wrong conclusions, biological and chemical and contaminant and sharps and equipment exposure, leakage of case and party information, court statements inconsistent with the report or opinions beyond scope, and personal safety risks in scene and traffic and night work. Control points are acting to procedure and validated methods with records, and pausing and reviewing and escalating per procedure.
entries.question: What are the main risks of this occupation?

entries.answer: Under the US definition growth over 2025—2035 is projected to be much faster than average (about 13%), with openings including a large share of replacement needs; a projection is not an individual opportunity, and actual opportunities depend on the technical investment and establishment of local law enforcement and forensic institutions. You can move to adjacent positions such as detectives and criminal investigators, police and detectives, police identification and records, fire inspection and fire investigation, private investigation, medical and clinical laboratory technology and compliance (which require relearning procedures and qualification requirements), or to laboratory quality management and technical management positions.
